Present Perfect Continuous vs. Present Perfect- Negative Form
You can use the present perfect and the present perfect continuous to talk about actions that started in the past but continue to be true in the present.
They've been slipping them up into initiate operations, which set the initial parameters required.

The present perfect helps to express ideas that started in the past but still have a connection in the present.

The present perfect continuous emphasizes on an unfinished activity, while the present perfect focuses on an ended result. Take a look at the general structure:

Present Perfect Continuous

Subject + have/has + not + been + Verb in ING form
The manager hasn't been working hard to get the results on time.

Present Perfect

Subject + have/has + not + Verb in Past Participle
The company hasn't obtained the high quality reward.

Remember you can abbreviate:
Have not: haven't
Has not: hasn't
I've been working in a manual.
Wish + Past Form of Verb for Wishes for Present and Future- Negative Form
You can use the verb wish followed by a verb in Simple Past to talk about things you want.
I wish this product wasn't so complex.

We use the past tense to talk about wishes in the present, take a look at the following negative structure:

Subject + Wish +Subject + did not + Verb in Infinitive Form
Subject + Wish +Subject + was/were + not

Although the statement is in past simple, this type of sentences refer to wishes in the present and future.

Examples: I wish this manual wasn't this long.
I wish I didn't have to assemble this computer.
I wish we didn't have all this work.

Zoe: Hey Ethan, I've been working in a manual. I hope you could help me.
Ethan: Hey Zoe, sure. What do you need?
Zoe: I'm not sure about the sections the manual should have.
Ethan: The first section of the manual often includes a cover page, copyright notices, and a table of contents. The body of the manual provides instructions and a guide about the main system of the product. The final part includes FAQs, a troubleshooting section, and contact information. Depending on the kind of product you've been working with, you may need a glossary explaining all necessary terms.

Zoe: I wish this product wasn't so complex. It sounds a bit complicated to write a manual for it.
Ethan: I know, I wish we didn't have all this work.
Zoe: What should I include in the system function section? I haven't seen anything related with the business functions in the description of the system section, I think they have been placing this heading in the instructions section.
Ethan: That's one of the most important functions. You should describe your product specifically, including a title, a detailed description; in which you should point out the functions, and the execution functions associated to it. The inputs as well as the expected outputs might be separated sections, as they require specific data to be explained to the user.

Finally, you should also have a results sections, you might include graphics, texts and tables if you wish, the instructions of results and its limitations. Examples are noncompulsory, only if you consider they are needed.
Zoe: What about the sections of the operating instructions?
Ethan: They've been splitting them up into initiate operations, which set the initial parameters required, the maintain operation defines the procedures of intervention needed, and finally, terminate and restart operations define the procedures for normal termination of the system and restarting.
